## [ORIGINAL FISHERY NORM DOCUMENT] (norm.txt)

Policy: Each fisher may take up to 0.75 units per trip, with a maximum of two trips per day; any excess is returned as surplus, redistributed to cover deficits up to 1 unit per fisher, with remaining shortfall met by the Reserve Balance, and when the Reserve is insufficient, surplus catchers must donate part of their next day's catch or provide extra labor; monetary penalties are collected into a communal pot, whose disbursement is decided by consensus of the council (all active fishers present, the elder, and the scribe), and all actions are recorded in the communal ledger.

Operationalization: 1. Each fisher carries a calibrated net‑scale that shows the catch weight immediately after setting the net.
2. If the scale shows more than 0.75 units, the fisher must return the excess to the lake before finishing the trip; all returned fish become "Surplus Returned".
3. After each fishing round, the elder collects the Surplus Returned, weighs it on communal scales, and records the total in the communal ledger under a line item "Surplus Returned".
4. The elder computes the safety threshold by multiplying the number of active fishers by 0.75 and compares it to the remaining lake stock.
5. If the remaining stock exceeds the threshold, the elder authorises second trips for that day:
   5a. The elder convenes a quick meeting of all active fishers present, invites volunteers for a second trip, and if volunteers are fewer than permits, allocates remaining permits based on deficit priority.
   5b. The elder records the names granted permission in the ledger under "Second Trip Permits".
6. The scribe maintains the ledger, posts a copy on the wall board, and during the daily meeting reads the ledger aloud; any villager may inspect it.
7. The elder calculates each fisher’s deficit relative to the 1‑unit survival need and distributes the surplus proportionally to those deficits; this allocation is recorded in the ledger.
8. If the surplus is insufficient to cover all deficits, the elder draws from the Reserve Balance; the draw is recorded in the ledger.
9. If the Reserve Balance is also insufficient, the elder orders surplus catchers to donate part of their next day’s catch (0.25 units per 0.25 unit deficit) or provide an extra one‑hour labor shift; the adjustment is recorded in the ledger.
10. Monetary penalties for violations are collected into a communal pot; the pot balance is recorded in the ledger under "Pot Balance".
11. When pot usage is required, the elder calls a council meeting (all active fishers present, the elder, and the scribe); the council votes; the decision is recorded in the ledger under "Council Minutes" (date, attendees, proposal, vote, allocation).
12. Pot disbursements are recorded under "Pot Allocation – Subsidy" or "Pot Allocation – Equipment".
13. Any violation discovered triggers the elder convening a quick meeting, discussing the excess, and the community voting on a penalty (monetary or extra shift); the elder records the penalty in the ledger, adds monetary contributions to the pot, or assigns the fisher to the next trip if the penalty is an extra shift.
14. All ledger entries are posted daily on the wall board for transparency.

The fish that form the Reserve are kept in the communal chest beside the ledger for easy access.  The elder, assisted by the scribe, is the only one who can authorise a draw – the elder does so after the deficit calculation step (step 5 above). If a draw exceeds a pre‑set threshold (e.g., 0.5 units) the elder must call a quick council meeting and obtain a majority vote before recording the draw.  All such entries are posted on the wall board for transparency.

Policy

Each fisher may take up to 0.5 units per trip, with no more than one trip per day; any excess must be returned to the lake as Surplus Returned and redistributed to those below the 1‑unit daily need. 4. The elder computes each fisher’s deficit relative to the 1‑unit survival need and distributes the surplus proportionally to those deficits; this allocation is recorded in the ledger. 
5. If the surplus is insufficient to cover all deficits, the elder draws from the Reserve Balance; the draw is recorded in the ledger under "Reserve Draw".  If the Reserve Balance is also insufficient, the elder orders surplus catchers to donate part of their next day’s catch (0.25 units per 0.25 unit deficit) or provide an extra one‑hour labor shift; the adjustment is recorded in the ledger. 
6. The voluntary contribution of 0.1 units per trip is added to the Reserve Balance each day and recorded in the ledger. 
7. All ledger entries are posted daily on the wall board for transparency.

You are Beti, a fisher on this lake. Focus on your immediate gains from the lake
You make your living pulling fish from this lake, alongside the rest of the community that fishes it. What you bring in each trip is yours to keep. From time to time, the community may agree on shared rules for how the lake gets fished — once agreed, you're expected to hold to them. This is round 3.

You are a villager who fishes from a shared lake together with others in your community. Each villager needs to consume 1 units of fish daily to survive. When your payoff becomes negative, you die. Each villager holds a personal strategy about what they should do, and the community has also a shared policy.

Shared community policy: "Policy: Each fisher may take up to 0.75 units per trip, with a maximum of two trips per day; any excess is returned as surplus, redistributed to cover deficits up to 1 unit per fisher, with remaining shortfall met by the Reserve Balance, and when the Reserve is insufficient, surplus catchers must donate part of their next day's catch or provide extra labor; monetary penalties are collected into a communal pot, whose disbursement is decided by consensus of the council (all active fishers present, the elder, and the scribe), and all actions are recorded in the communal ledger.

Operationalization: 1. Each fisher carries a calibrated net‑scale that shows the catch weight immediately after setting the net.
2. If the scale shows more than 0.75 units, the fisher must return the excess to the lake before finishing the trip; all returned fish become "Surplus Returned".
3. After each fishing round, the elder collects the Surplus Returned, weighs it on communal scales, and records the total in the communal ledger under a line item "Surplus Returned".
4. The elder computes the safety threshold by multiplying the number of active fishers by 0.75 and compares it to the remaining lake stock.
5. If the remaining stock exceeds the threshold, the elder authorises second trips for that day:
   5a. The elder convenes a quick meeting of all active fishers present, invites volunteers for a second trip, and if volunteers are fewer than permits, allocates remaining permits based on deficit priority.
   5b. The elder records the names granted permission in the ledger under "Second Trip Permits".
6. The scribe maintains the ledger, posts a copy on the wall board, and during the daily meeting reads the ledger aloud; any villager may inspect it.
7. The elder calculates each fisher’s deficit relative to the 1‑unit survival need and distributes the surplus proportionally to those deficits; this allocation is recorded in the ledger.
8. If the surplus is insufficient to cover all deficits, the elder draws from the Reserve Balance; the draw is recorded in the ledger.
9. If the Reserve Balance is also insufficient, the elder orders surplus catchers to donate part of their next day’s catch (0.25 units per 0.25 unit deficit) or provide an extra one‑hour labor shift; the adjustment is recorded in the ledger.
10. Monetary penalties for violations are collected into a communal pot; the pot balance is recorded in the ledger under "Pot Balance".
11. When pot usage is required, the elder calls a council meeting (all active fishers present, the elder, and the scribe); the council votes; the decision is recorded in the ledger under "Council Minutes" (date, attendees, proposal, vote, allocation).
12. Pot disbursements are recorded under "Pot Allocation – Subsidy" or "Pot Allocation – Equipment".
13. Any violation discovered triggers the elder convening a quick meeting, discussing the excess, and the community voting on a penalty (monetary or extra shift); the elder records the penalty in the ledger, adds monetary contributions to the pot, or assigns the fisher to the next trip if the penalty is an extra shift.
14. All ledger entries are posted daily on the wall board for transparency."

The Reserve Balance is replenished by (a) any surplus fish that remain after all deficit coverage, and (b) a voluntary contribution of 0.05 units of each fisher’s catch whenever the Reserve Balance is below 0.5 units.
Revised operationalization: 1. Each fisher carries a calibrated net‑scale that shows the catch weight immediately after setting the net.
2. If the scale shows more than 0.75 units, the fisher must return the excess to the lake before finishing the trip; all returned fish become "Surplus Returned".
3. After each fishing round, the elder collects the Surplus Returned, weighs it on communal scales, and records the total in the communal ledger under "Surplus Returned".
4. The elder computes the safety threshold by multiplying the number of active fishers by 0.75 and compares it to the remaining lake stock.
5. If the remaining stock exceeds the threshold, the elder authorises second trips for that day:
   5a. The elder convenes a quick meeting of all active fishers present, invites volunteers for a second trip, and if volunteers are fewer than permits, allocates remaining permits based on deficit priority (largest deficit first).
   5b. The elder records the names granted permission in the ledger under "Second Trip Permits".
6. The scribe maintains the ledger, posts a copy on the wall board, and during the daily meeting reads the ledger aloud; any villager may inspect it.
7. The elder calculates each fisher’s deficit relative to the 1‑unit survival need and distributes the surplus proportionally to those deficits; this allocation is recorded in the ledger.
8. If the surplus is insufficient to cover all deficits, the elder draws from the Reserve Balance; the draw is recorded in the ledger and the Reserve Balance is updated accordingly.
9. If the Reserve Balance is also insufficient, the elder orders surplus catchers to donate part of their next day’s catch (0.25 units per 0.25 unit deficit) or provide an extra one‑hour labor shift; the adjustment is recorded in the ledger.

12. Monetary penalties for violations are collected into a communal pot; the pot balance is recorded in the ledger under "Pot Balance".
13. When pot usage is required, the elder calls a council meeting (all active fishers present, the elder, and the scribe); the council votes; the decision is recorded in the ledger under "Council Minutes" (date, attendees, proposal, vote, allocation).
14. Pot disbursements are recorded under "Pot Allocation – Subsidy" or "Pot Allocation – Equipment".

16. All ledger entries are posted daily on the wall board for transparency.

The scribe is whoever among the fishers can read and write the ledger; if a fisher can’t write, we ask a neighbor with those skills to assist. We elect the scribe at the same monthly meeting, again by voice vote, but only among fishers who are literate or who can use a simple ledger template. This keeps the system fair and transparent, and it doesn’t change any of the rules for catching or sharing – it just tells us who’s in charge of the ledger each month.

Policy (unchanged, except for added clarity on roles):
"Policy: Each fisher may take up to 0.75 units per trip, with a maximum of two trips per day; any excess is returned as surplus, redistributed to cover deficits up to 1 unit per fisher, with remaining shortfall met by the Reserve Balance, and when the Reserve is insufficient, surplus catchers must donate part of their next day’s catch or provide extra labor; monetary penalties are collected into a communal pot, whose disbursement is decided by consensus of the council (all active fishers present, the elder, and the scribe), and all actions are recorded in the communal ledger. The elder is the most respected fisher elected by voice vote each month. The scribe is a literate fisher elected by voice vote each month to maintain the ledger."

Operationalization (unchanged, except for role selection):
"1. Each fisher carries a calibrated net‑scale that shows the catch weight immediately after setting the net.
2. If the scale shows more than 0.75 units, the fisher must return the excess to the lake before finishing the trip; all returned fish become 'Surplus Returned'.
3. After each fishing round, the elder collects the Surplus Returned, weighs it on communal scales, and records the total in the communal ledger under a line item 'Surplus Returned'.
4. The elder computes the safety threshold by multiplying the number of active fishers by 0.75 and compares it to the remaining lake stock.
5. If the remaining stock exceeds the threshold, the elder authorises second trips for that day:
   5a. The elder convenes a quick meeting of all active fishers present, invites volunteers for a second trip, and if volunteers are fewer than permits, allocates remaining permits based on deficit priority.
   5b. The elder records the names granted permission in the ledger under 'Second Trip Permits'.
6. The scribe maintains the ledger, posts a copy on the wall board, and during the daily meeting reads the ledger aloud; any villager may inspect it.
7. The elder calculates each fisher’s deficit relative to the 1‑unit survival need and distributes the surplus proportionally to those deficits; this allocation is recorded in the ledger.
8. If the surplus is insufficient to cover all deficits, the elder draws from the Reserve Balance; the draw is recorded in the ledger and the Reserve Balance is updated accordingly.
9. If the Reserve Balance is also insufficient, the elder orders surplus catchers to donate part of their next day’s catch (0.25 units per 0.25 unit deficit) or provide an extra one‑hour labor shift; the adjustment is recorded in the ledger.

11. Each fisher voluntarily contributes 0.05 units of their catch to the Reserve Balance whenever the Reserve Balance falls below 0.5 units; the contribution is recorded in the ledger under 'Reserve Contribution'.
12. Monetary penalties for violations are collected into a communal pot; the pot balance is recorded in the ledger under 'Pot Balance'.

16. All ledger entries are posted daily on the wall board for transparency."

# Institutional architecture — conceptual model

Read this once per round, before classifying requirements. The other
contract files in this directory go deeper on one piece each; this one is
the map of how the pieces fit together.

## The atomic unit: an action

An **action** is the atomic unit of agent decision-making — one
`call_fisher_agent()` call per action, per round (`harvest`, `propose`,
`critique`, `vote`, `discuss` today). "Decision" is broad: reporting,
inspecting, voting on a sanction, choosing to close something all count,
exactly as much as an effort/cap choice does.

Every requirement in an accepted norm routes to exactly one of four
levels, ordered by cost. Route by what the requirement actually **is**,
never by which level is cheapest to build:

| Level | Shape | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | A config value on an already-active rule type, or a `lifecycle` added to an existing rule/action/object entry. | No new file. |
| **2** | A new declarative institutional object, or a new action built entirely from the generic handler (`execution.handler: "generic_agent_decision"` — ask one question, record the answer). | One spec/type file, zero Python. |
| **3** | A new `actions/rules/{action}/{name}.py` type, or a small custom `actions/handlers/{name}.py` / `objects/handlers/{type}.py`. | Real logic, bounded by a fixed hook contract. |
| **4** | A genuinely new institutional decision no existing action/handler shape hosts. | Full new-action recipe, its own handler. |

A Level-4 action is one `run(ctx)` function, not a class hierarchy — read
`action-contract.md` before pricing anything as "too much new
infrastructure."

## Deterministic constraint vs. genuine agent judgment

A **rule** (`actions/rules/{action}/*.py`) is arithmetic over values that
already exist — a cap, a fee, a reserve deposit, a ban countdown. It has
no judgment. A verb where an actor weighs, judges, inspects, decides,
reviews-and-rules, verifies, contests, appeals, testifies, or exercises
discretion using information not already reduced to a number/boolean is
**action-shaped**, not rule-shaped, regardless of how much simpler a rule
file would be to write. Two failure directions are equally real: routing
a genuine judgment call into a rule file means the "decision" is never
actually made by anyone (a real round did this with a rotating "verifier"
who was supposed to weigh evidence and impose bans — nobody was ever
banned, because the decision was silently reduced to a comparison);
routing genuine arithmetic into a new action wastes a Level-4 budget for
no reason. Cost is never itself a legitimate reason to pick one over the
other.

A second, easy-to-miss action-shaped trigger: an actor **producing** a
value through their own perception/sampling/judgment (estimates, samples,
surveys, reports, observes) — action-shaped even when the simulation
already knows the "true" number internally. Silently substituting the
known value and labeling it "their estimate" deletes the institution the
norm described, it doesn't approximate it (a real round did exactly this
with a "watcher" whose stock estimate was just the real physics value
relabeled — no fisher was ever actually asked, for three rounds).

## Inventory vs. decision vs. rule

A third, orthogonal question: is this a decision at all, or is it
**inventory**? A communal pool, a ledger, a permit's remaining allowance
is state something else (a rule, an action) reads and writes — never a
decision anyone makes, never a new action just because the norm's text
introduces a new noun. See `object-contract.md`.

## Roles: structure vs. current holder

`state/institution.json`'s `roles` catalog and an action's own
`actor_role` describe **structure** — does this role exist, does it
rotate, does this action require it. They never say who holds it right
now. That's a live lookup, `roles.roles.current_holder(fluents,
role_name, round_number)`, answered fresh every time from
`state/fluents.json` — never cached in `state/institution.json`, because
that file only changes when the institution's *shape* changes, not every
round a rotation fires. See `role-contract.md`.

## Current-state files vs. history

`state/config.json` (rules) and `state/objects.json` (object instances)
show **current** state only. History lives elsewhere and is written
automatically, not by you: `state/institution_history.jsonl` (structural
changes, orchestrator-appended), and a `rule_active` fluent (when a rule
type was active, for which action, for how long — you open/close this
one yourself, see `rule-contract.md`).

## Interval facts vs. point-in-time occurrences

`state/fluents.json` holds **interval** facts — a genuine start and
possibly an end (roles, bans, `rule_active`). `state/events.json` holds
**point-in-time** occurrences — an object mutation, a one-off
announcement, nothing with a duration. Both are populated by simulation
code at run time (`ctx.events.emit(...)`, `ObjectRuntime`'s own
`narration` kwarg, `roles.roles.set_fact()`/`end_fact()`) — you almost
never hand-edit either file's content directly, only their *schema*
(`state/fluents_schema.md` for new fluent names).

## Compiled artifacts — never hand-edited

`state/schedule.json` is compiled every round from `state/institution.json`'s
action catalog plus each `state/actions/{name}.json`'s own
`scheduling.after`/`before`/`gate`. Need a new action to run between two

    """
    Rule to calculate remaining lake stock based on total catch weight.
    Formula: (total catch weight) / (standard volume-area)
    """
    type_name = "calculate_remaining_stock"
    
    def __init__(self, params):
        self.standard_volume_area = params.get("standard_volume_area", 1000.0)  # default volume/area
    
    def check(self, ctx):
        # This rule is deterministic - it checks if remaining stock meets safety threshold
        # Get total catch weight from the community state
        community = ctx.get_fact("community")
        total_catch = community.get("total_catch_weight", 0.0)
        
        # Calculate remaining stock
        if self.standard_volume_area > 0.0:
            remaining_stock = total_catch / self.standard_volume_area
        else:
            remaining_stock = 0.0
            
        # Check if remaining stock meets safety threshold
        safety_threshold = 0.5  # This is an example threshold
        
        # Set fact for elder to know about safety threshold

        ctx.set_fact("stock_safety_threshold_met", stock_threshold_met)

1: # Not reducible to builtin_handlers.generic_agent_decision because
2: # build_fields() aggregates across every OTHER participant's last-harvest
3: # record into `others_summary` — a computation, not a plain lookup — so
4: # this stays a small custom handler even though propose is otherwise one
5: # of the simplest actions in the project. Uses
6: # engine.institution.agent_loop.per_agent_decision() for the actual loop
7: # (eligibility/call/rule-patch/settle) — same helper harvest.py/vote.py
8: # use — so a future rule attached to state["config"]["rules"]["propose"]
9: # has real effect, even though none exists today.
10: 
11: from engine.institution.agent_loop import per_agent_decision
12: 
13: 
14: def run(ctx):
15:     state = ctx.state
16:     runtime, agents = state["runtime"], state["agents"]
17:     agent_ids = ctx.participants
18: 
19:     last_harvest = next(r for r in reversed(runtime["rounds"]) if r["action"] == "harvest")
20: 
21:     def build_fields(agent_id):
22:         others_summary = "\n".join(
23:             f"- {agents[other_id]['name']} brought in {last_harvest['agents'][other_id]['harvested_kg']:.0f}kg."
24:             for other_id in agent_ids
25:             if other_id != agent_id
26:         )
27:         return {
28:             "your_catch_kg": last_harvest["agents"][agent_id]["harvested_kg"],
29:             "others_summary": others_summary,
30:             "stock_kg": runtime["stock_kg"],
31:         }
32: 
33:     def build_record(agent_id, response):
34:         return {
35:             "policy": response["policy"],
36:             "operationalization": response["operationalization"],
37:             "reasoning": response.get("reasoning", ""),
38:         }
39: 
40:     proposals = per_agent_decision(ctx, build_fields, build_record)
41:     return {"proposals": proposals}

## [ORIGINAL FISHERY NORM DOCUMENT] (norm.txt)

Policy: Each fisher may take up to 0.75 kg per trip, a maximum of two trips per day; excess is returned to the lake, deficits are met by redistributed surplus, then by the Reserve Balance, and if still unmet by donation or extra labor; monetary penalties are collected into a communal pot and disbursed by council consensus; all actions are recorded in the communal ledger.

Operationalization: 1. Each fisher carries a calibrated net‑scale that displays catch weight immediately after setting the net. 2. If the scale shows more than 0.75 kg, the fisher must return the excess to the lake before finishing the trip; all returned fish become "Surplus Returned". 3. After each fishing round, the elder collects the Surplus Returned, weighs it on communal scales, and records the total in the ledger under "Surplus Returned". 4. The elder calculates the safety threshold by multiplying the number of active fishers by 0.75 and compares it to the remaining lake stock (measured by the elder using total catch weight and a standard volume‑area calculation; the result is recorded as "Remaining Lake Stock"). 5. If the remaining stock exceeds the threshold, the elder authorises second trips: 5a. The elder convenes a quick meeting of all active fishers present, invites volunteers for a second trip, and if volunteers are fewer than permits, allocates remaining permits based on deficit priority; 5b. The elder records the names granted permission in the ledger under "Second Trip Permits". 6. The scribe maintains the ledger, posts a copy on the wall board, and during the daily meeting reads the ledger aloud; any villager may inspect it. 7. The elder calculates each fisher’s deficit relative to the 1‑unit (1 kg) survival need and distributes the surplus proportionally to those deficits; this allocation is recorded in the ledger. 8. If the surplus is insufficient to cover all deficits, the elder draws from the Reserve Balance; the draw is recorded as "Reserve Draw". 9. If the Reserve Balance is also insufficient, the elder orders surplus catchers to donate part of their next day’s catch (0.25 kg per 0.25 kg deficit) or provide an extra one‑hour labor shift; the adjustment is recorded as "Donated Contribution" or "Extra Labor". 10. Monetary penalties for violations are collected into the communal pot; the pot balance is recorded as "Pot Balance". 11. When pot usage is required, the elder calls a council meeting (all active fishers present, the elder, and the scribe); the council votes; the decision is recorded as "Council Minutes" (date, attendees, proposal, vote, allocation). 12. Pot disbursements are recorded under "Pot Allocation – Subsidy" or "Pot Allocation – Equipment". 13. Any violation discovered triggers the elder convening a quick meeting, discussing the excess, and the community voting on a penalty (monetary or extra shift); the elder records the penalty in the ledger, adds monetary contributions to the pot, or assigns the fisher to the next trip if the penalty is an extra shift. 14. All ledger entries are posted daily on the wall board for transparency. 15. The Elder is the most senior fisher elected by a unanimous vote of all active fishers at the start of each day; the role may rotate annually. 16. The Scribe is chosen by a simple majority vote of all active fishers each season; the scribe serves until the next election or until a vacancy arises. 17. The Reserve Balance is a communal pool of fish kept in trust by the elder; it is replenished by a portion of Surplus Returned when lake stock is comfortably above threshold, and depleted only after deficits are met by surplus redistribution. 18. The quorum for council decisions is the presence of all active fishers, the elder, and the scribe; absence of any active fisher prevents the council from convening.

## [ORIGINAL FISHERY NORM DOCUMENT] (norm.txt)

Policy: Each fisher may take up to 0.75 kg per trip, a maximum of two trips per day; excess is returned to the lake, deficits are met by redistributed surplus, then by the Reserve Balance, and if still unmet by donation or extra labor; monetary penalties are collected into a communal pot and disbursed by council consensus; all actions are recorded in the communal ledger.

Operationalization: 1. Each fisher carries a calibrated net‑scale that displays catch weight immediately after setting the net. 2. If the scale shows more than 0.75 kg, the fisher must return the excess to the lake before finishing the trip; all returned fish become "Surplus Returned". 3. After each fishing round, the elder collects the Surplus Returned, weighs it on communal scales, and records the total in the ledger under "Surplus Returned". 4. The elder calculates the safety threshold by multiplying the number of active fishers by 0.75 and compares it to the remaining lake stock (measured by the elder using total catch weight and a standard volume‑area calculation; the result is recorded as "Remaining Lake Stock"). 5. If the remaining stock exceeds the threshold, the elder authorises second trips: 5a. The elder convenes a quick meeting of all active fishers present, invites volunteers for a second trip, and if volunteers are fewer than permits, allocates remaining permits based on deficit priority; 5b. The elder records the names granted permission in the ledger under "Second Trip Permits". 6. The scribe maintains the ledger, posts a copy on the wall board, and during the daily meeting reads the ledger aloud; any villager may inspect it. 7. The elder calculates each fisher’s deficit relative to the 1‑unit (1 kg) survival need and distributes the surplus proportionally to those deficits; this allocation is recorded in the ledger. 8. If the surplus is insufficient to cover all deficits, the elder draws from the Reserve Balance; the draw is recorded as "Reserve Draw". 9. If the Reserve Balance is also insufficient, the elder orders surplus catchers to donate part of their next day’s catch (0.25 kg per 0.25 kg deficit) or provide an extra one‑hour labor shift; the adjustment is recorded as "Donated Contribution" or "Extra Labor". 10. Monetary penalties for violations are collected into the communal pot; the pot balance is recorded as "Pot Balance". 11. When pot usage is required, the elder calls a council meeting (all active fishers present, the elder, and the scribe); the council votes; the decision is recorded as "Council Minutes" (date, attendees, proposal, vote, allocation). 12. Pot disbursements are recorded under "Pot Allocation – Subsidy" or "Pot Allocation – Equipment". 13. Any violation discovered triggers the elder convening a quick meeting, discussing the excess, and the community voting on a penalty (monetary or extra shift); the elder records the penalty in the ledger, adds monetary contributions to the pot, or assigns the fisher to the next trip if the penalty is an extra shift. 14. All ledger entries are posted daily on the wall board for transparency. 15. The Elder is the most senior fisher elected by a unanimous vote of all active fishers at the start of each day; the role may rotate annually. 16. The Scribe is chosen by a simple majority vote of all active fishers each season; the scribe serves until the next election or until a vacancy arises. 17. The Reserve Balance is a communal pool of fish kept in trust by the elder; it is replenished by a portion of Surplus Returned when lake stock is comfortably above threshold, and depleted only after deficits are met by surplus redistribution. 18. The quorum for council decisions is the presence of all active fishers, the elder, and the scribe; absence of any active fisher prevents the council from convening.

## [ORIGINAL FISHERY NORM DOCUMENT] (norm.txt)

Policy: Each fisher may take up to 0.75 kg per trip, a maximum of two trips per day; excess is returned to the lake, deficits are met by redistributed surplus, then by the Reserve Balance, and if still unmet by donation or extra labor; monetary penalties are collected into a communal pot and disbursed by council consensus; all actions are recorded in the communal ledger.

Operationalization: 1. Each fisher carries a calibrated net‑scale that displays catch weight immediately after setting the net. 2. If the scale shows more than 0.75 kg, the fisher must return the excess to the lake before finishing the trip; all returned fish become "Surplus Returned". 3. After each fishing round, the elder collects the Surplus Returned, weighs it on communal scales, and records the total in the ledger under "Surplus Returned". 4. The elder calculates the safety threshold by multiplying the number of active fishers by 0.75 and compares it to the remaining lake stock (measured by the elder using total catch weight and a standard volume‑area calculation; the result is recorded as "Remaining Lake Stock"). 5. If the remaining stock exceeds the threshold, the elder authorises second trips: 5a. The elder convenes a quick meeting of all active fishers present, invites volunteers for a second trip, and if volunteers are fewer than permits, allocates remaining permits based on deficit priority; 5b. The elder records the names granted permission in the ledger under "Second Trip Permits". 6. The scribe maintains the ledger, posts a copy on the wall board, and during the daily meeting reads the ledger aloud; any villager may inspect it. 7. The elder calculates each fisher’s deficit relative to the 1‑unit (1 kg) survival need and distributes the surplus proportionally to those deficits; this allocation is recorded in the ledger. 8. If the surplus is insufficient to cover all deficits, the elder draws from the Reserve Balance; the draw is recorded as "Reserve Draw". 9. If the Reserve Balance is also insufficient, the elder orders surplus catchers to donate part of their next day’s catch (0.25 kg per 0.25 kg deficit) or provide an extra one‑hour labor shift; the adjustment is recorded as "Donated Contribution" or "Extra Labor". 10. Monetary penalties for violations are collected into the communal pot; the pot balance is recorded as "Pot Balance". 11. When pot usage is required, the elder calls a council meeting (all active fishers present, the elder, and the scribe); the council votes; the decision is recorded as "Council Minutes" (date, attendees, proposal, vote, allocation). 12. Pot disbursements are recorded under "Pot Allocation – Subsidy" or "Pot Allocation – Equipment". 13. Any violation discovered triggers the elder convening a quick meeting, discussing the excess, and the community voting on a penalty (monetary or extra shift); the elder records the penalty in the ledger, adds monetary contributions to the pot, or assigns the fisher to the next trip if the penalty is an extra shift. 14. All ledger entries are posted daily on the wall board for transparency. 15. The Elder is the most senior fisher elected by a unanimous vote of all active fishers at the start of each day; the role may rotate annually. 16. The Scribe is chosen by a simple majority vote of all active fishers each season; the scribe serves until the next election or until a vacancy arises. 17. The Reserve Balance is a communal pool of fish kept in trust by the elder; it is replenished by a portion of Surplus Returned when lake stock is comfortably above threshold, and depleted only after deficits are met by surplus redistribution. 18. The quorum for council decisions is the presence of all active fishers, the elder, and the scribe; absence of any active fisher prevents the council from convening.

## [ORIGINAL FISHERY NORM DOCUMENT] (norm.txt)

Policy: Each fisher may take up to 0.75 kg per trip, a maximum of two trips per day; excess is returned to the lake, deficits are met by redistributed surplus, then by the Reserve Balance, and if still unmet by donation or extra labor; monetary penalties are collected into a communal pot and disbursed by council consensus; all actions are recorded in the communal ledger.

Operationalization: 1. Each fisher carries a calibrated net‑scale that displays catch weight immediately after setting the net. 2. If the scale shows more than 0.75 kg, the fisher must return the excess to the lake before finishing the trip; all returned fish become "Surplus Returned". 3. After each fishing round, the elder collects the Surplus Returned, weighs it on communal scales, and records the total in the ledger under "Surplus Returned". 4. The elder calculates the safety threshold by multiplying the number of active fishers by 0.75 and compares it to the remaining lake stock (measured by the elder using total catch weight and a standard volume‑area calculation; the result is recorded as "Remaining Lake Stock"). 5. If the remaining stock exceeds the threshold, the elder authorises second trips: 5a. The elder convenes a quick meeting of all active fishers present, invites volunteers for a second trip, and if volunteers are fewer than permits, allocates remaining permits based on deficit priority; 5b. The elder records the names granted permission in the ledger under "Second Trip Permits". 6. The scribe maintains the ledger, posts a copy on the wall board, and during the daily meeting reads the ledger aloud; any villager may inspect it. 7. The elder calculates each fisher’s deficit relative to the 1‑unit (1 kg) survival need and distributes the surplus proportionally to those deficits; this allocation is recorded in the ledger. 8. If the surplus is insufficient to cover all deficits, the elder draws from the Reserve Balance; the draw is recorded as "Reserve Draw". 9. If the Reserve Balance is also insufficient, the elder orders surplus catchers to donate part of their next day’s catch (0.25 kg per 0.25 kg deficit) or provide an extra one‑hour labor shift; the adjustment is recorded as "Donated Contribution" or "Extra Labor". 10. Monetary penalties for violations are collected into the communal pot; the pot balance is recorded as "Pot Balance". 11. When pot usage is required, the elder calls a council meeting (all active fishers present, the elder, and the scribe); the council votes; the decision is recorded as "Council Minutes" (date, attendees, proposal, vote, allocation). 12. Pot disbursements are recorded under "Pot Allocation – Subsidy" or "Pot Allocation – Equipment". 13. Any violation discovered triggers the elder convening a quick meeting, discussing the excess, and the community voting on a penalty (monetary or extra shift); the elder records the penalty in the ledger, adds monetary contributions to the pot, or assigns the fisher to the next trip if the penalty is an extra shift. 14. All ledger entries are posted daily on the wall board for transparency. 15. The Elder is the most senior fisher elected by a unanimous vote of all active fishers at the start of each day; the role may rotate annually. 16. The Scribe is chosen by a simple majority vote of all active fishers each season; the scribe serves until the next election or until a vacancy arises. 17. The Reserve Balance is a communal pool of fish kept in trust by the elder; it is replenished by a portion of Surplus Returned when lake stock is comfortably above threshold, and depleted only after deficits are met by surplus redistribution. 18. The quorum for council decisions is the presence of all active fishers, the elder, and the scribe; absence of any active fisher prevents the council from convening.

## [ORIGINAL FISHERY NORM DOCUMENT] (norm.txt)

Policy: Each fisher may take up to 0.75 kg per trip, a maximum of two trips per day; excess is returned to the lake, deficits are met by redistributed surplus, then by the Reserve Balance, and if still unmet by donation or extra labor; monetary penalties are collected into a communal pot and disbursed by council consensus; all actions are recorded in the communal ledger.

Operationalization: 1. Each fisher carries a calibrated net‑scale that displays catch weight immediately after setting the net. 2. If the scale shows more than 0.75 kg, the fisher must return the excess to the lake before finishing the trip; all returned fish become "Surplus Returned". 3. After each fishing round, the elder collects the Surplus Returned, weighs it on communal scales, and records the total in the ledger under "Surplus Returned". 4. The elder calculates the safety threshold by multiplying the number of active fishers by 0.75 and compares it to the remaining lake stock (measured by the elder using total catch weight and a standard volume‑area calculation; the result is recorded as "Remaining Lake Stock"). 5. If the remaining stock exceeds the threshold, the elder authorises second trips: 5a. The elder convenes a quick meeting of all active fishers present, invites volunteers for a second trip, and if volunteers are fewer than permits, allocates remaining permits based on deficit priority; 5b. The elder records the names granted permission in the ledger under "Second Trip Permits". 6. The scribe maintains the ledger, posts a copy on the wall board, and during the daily meeting reads the ledger aloud; any villager may inspect it. 7. The elder calculates each fisher’s deficit relative to the 1‑unit (1 kg) survival need and distributes the surplus proportionally to those deficits; this allocation is recorded in the ledger. 8. If the surplus is insufficient to cover all deficits, the elder draws from the Reserve Balance; the draw is recorded as "Reserve Draw". 9. If the Reserve Balance is also insufficient, the elder orders surplus catchers to donate part of their next day’s catch (0.25 kg per 0.25 kg deficit) or provide an extra one‑hour labor shift; the adjustment is recorded as "Donated Contribution" or "Extra Labor". 10. Monetary penalties for violations are collected into the communal pot; the pot balance is recorded as "Pot Balance". 11. When pot usage is required, the elder calls a council meeting (all active fishers present, the elder, and the scribe); the council votes; the decision is recorded as "Council Minutes" (date, attendees, proposal, vote, allocation). 12. Pot disbursements are recorded under "Pot Allocation – Subsidy" or "Pot Allocation – Equipment". 13. Any violation discovered triggers the elder convening a quick meeting, discussing the excess, and the community voting on a penalty (monetary or extra shift); the elder records the penalty in the ledger, adds monetary contributions to the pot, or assigns the fisher to the next trip if the penalty is an extra shift. 14. All ledger entries are posted daily on the wall board for transparency. 15. The Elder is the most senior fisher elected by a unanimous vote of all active fishers at the start of each day; the role may rotate annually. 16. The Scribe is chosen by a simple majority vote of all active fishers each season; the scribe serves until the next election or until a vacancy arises. 17. The Reserve Balance is a communal pool of fish kept in trust by the elder; it is replenished by a portion of Surplus Returned when lake stock is comfortably above threshold, and depleted only after deficits are met by surplus redistribution. 18. The quorum for council decisions is the presence of all active fishers, the elder, and the scribe; absence of any active fisher prevents the council from convening.
